An interactive book in four chapters

From Search to Generative AI

How do you improve a neural network when you cannot easily work out which way to change it? This book shows how evolution-style search can do it, why keeping variety matters, and how these ideas now work together with large language models.

It is written for a high-school student who has learned probability distributions, derivatives and the basics of neural networks, and has a rough picture of what is inside an LLM. You do not need to know anything about evolutionary algorithms yet.

Start reading →

What you already know, and how it is used here

Probability distributions

A normal distribution N(μ, σ²) describes where random values tend to land. In this book a distribution describes where to try candidate solutions: its mean is the current best guess, and its spread controls how boldly we explore.

Derivatives

Gradient descent follows the slope of a loss. Evolution needs no slope at all: it only compares scores. That makes it useful when the score is noisy, jumps around, or comes from a whole game played to the end.

Neural networks

A network is layers of weights plus activation functions. Here, all its weights are written out as one long list of numbers, and that list is what evolution changes. Some methods also add new neurons and connections.

LLMs

An LLM turns text into tokens, maps them to embeddings, and outputs a probability distribution over the next token. Chapter 4 uses LLMs both as something to improve and as a smart way to suggest changes.

Two kinds of distribution. An LLM's distribution says which word might come next. An evolution strategy's distribution says which solution to try next. Both are probability distributions, but they describe different things.

How to read each chapter

1 · Predict

Before you touch a slider or press Play, guess what will happen. A wrong guess is the fastest way to learn.

2 · Play

Every demo runs a real, small version of the algorithm in your browser. Run it several times: randomness means each run differs.

3 · Check

Dotted words show a definition when you hover or tap them. Each chapter ends with a recap and review questions you can open to check your answers.

Markers such as “§3.2” or “Ch 7” point to sections and chapters of the textbook these notes follow: Neuroevolution by Risi, Tang, Ha and Miikkulainen. You do not need the textbook to follow along. Unfamiliar terms are collected in the glossary.

Quick reference

Glossary

Plain-language meanings of the terms used in this book, grouped by the chapter where they first matter.

Search basics Chapter 1

Optimization
Looking for the input that gives the best score. Training a neural network is optimization: find the weights with the lowest loss.
Fitness
A single number that says how good a candidate is, such as the distance a robot walks. Higher is better. Unlike a loss, it never needs a derivative.
Fitness landscape
A picture of fitness over all possible candidates: hills are good solutions, valleys are bad ones. Search means trying to climb to the highest hill.
Local optimum
A hilltop that is higher than everything nearby but not the highest overall. Both gradient descent and evolution can get stuck on one.
Population / individual
The group of candidates being tested at once. Each member is an individual.
Generation
One round of the loop: score everyone, choose parents, create the next population.
Selection
Letting better-scoring individuals have more children. Strong selection is fast but loses variety.
Mutation
A small random change to a candidate, often adding a little Gaussian noise to its numbers.
Crossover
Making a child by mixing parts of two parents.
Genotype / phenotype
The genotype is the stored description that evolution edits, such as a list of weights. The phenotype is what it builds and what gets tested, such as the working network.
Evolutionary algorithm (EA)
Any method that repeats: make candidates, score them, keep and vary the better ones.
Genetic algorithm (GA)
An EA that uses selection, crossover and mutation on a population of encoded candidates.
Evolution strategy (ES)
An EA that samples candidates from a probability distribution, usually a normal distribution, then moves that distribution toward the better samples.
Covariance
Describes the shape of a multi-dimensional normal distribution: how stretched it is and in which direction. CMA-ES learns this shape so that it searches along promising directions.
CMA-ES
An evolution strategy that learns both the mean and the covariance of its search distribution from its best samples.
OpenAI-ES
An evolution strategy that combines random perturbations, weighted by how well they scored, into an estimate of the gradient, without ever calculating a derivative.
Rank-based fitness shaping
Using each candidate's rank instead of its raw score, so one extreme score cannot dominate an update.
Pareto front
When there are several goals (fast and cheap), the set of solutions where you cannot improve one goal without worsening another.
NSGA-II
A popular evolutionary algorithm for several goals at once. It keeps the best Pareto fronts and prefers solutions that are spread out along them.

Evolving networks Chapter 2

Neuroevolution
Using evolutionary algorithms to find a neural network's weights, its structure, or both.
Topology
The structure of a network: how many neurons there are and which ones connect.
TWEANN
Topology and Weight Evolving Artificial Neural Network: a method that evolves structure as well as weights.
Direct / indirect encoding
A direct encoding lists every weight or connection. An indirect encoding stores a shorter rule that grows the network, so one change can affect many connections.
NEAT
NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies. It starts with tiny networks and gradually adds neurons and connections only when they help.
Innovation number
A label NEAT gives each new connection, so genes from two different networks can be lined up during crossover.
Speciation
Grouping similar networks into species that mainly compete among themselves, giving new ideas time to improve before they are judged against the best.
Policy
A rule, often a neural network, that maps what an agent senses to the action it takes.
Reward / rollout
A reward is a score received while acting. A rollout is one full trial, such as one attempt at a walking course. Fitness is often the total reward of a rollout.

Diversity Chapter 3

Premature convergence
When the whole population becomes nearly identical too early, so the search stops exploring before finding the best region.
Deception
When following the score leads away from the best solution, like a maze where heading straight for the exit runs into a dead end.
Behavior characterization
A short list of numbers describing what a candidate does, such as where a robot ends up. Used to measure how different two behaviors are.
Novelty search
Rewarding candidates for behaving differently from what has been seen before, instead of for scoring well.
Archive
A saved collection of past candidates, used to tell whether a new behavior is genuinely new.
Stepping stone
An intermediate solution that is not good by itself but makes a better solution reachable later.
Quality diversity (QD)
Methods that look for many different kinds of solution, each as good as possible for its kind.
MAP-Elites
A QD method that divides behaviors into a grid of cells and keeps the best candidate found in each cell.
Ensemble
Several models combined, for example by voting or averaging, which is often more reliable than any single one.

Generative AI Chapter 4

Token
A piece of text, such as a word or part of a word, that an LLM reads and writes one at a time.
Embedding
A vector that represents a token, sentence or program so that similar things are close together. Distances between embeddings can measure diversity.
Temperature
A number that reshapes a model's output distribution before sampling. Low temperature makes the most likely choice dominate; high temperature makes choices more random.
Prompt
The text given to an LLM to steer its answer. Prompts can be evolved like any other candidate.
Fine-tuning
Training an already-trained model further on a narrower task.
Model merging
Building a new model by combining the weights or layers of existing models.
LLM mutation / crossover
Asking an LLM to make a sensible change to a program or prompt (mutation), or to write a new one in the style of several examples (crossover).
Latent vector
The list of random-looking numbers a generator turns into an output, such as a game level. Searching over it searches over outputs.
GAN
Generative Adversarial Network: a generator and a critic trained against each other until the generator produces realistic outputs.
World model
A learned simulator that predicts what happens next, so an agent can practice inside its own “dream” of the environment.
